newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to compromise on U.S. insurance row - sources.
newsitem.headline: Japan to compromise on U.S. insurance row - sources.

text.p: In a compromise with the United States, Japan will delay the entry of domestic insurance companies into a sector especially profitable to foreign firms and will begin to deregulate its large non-life insurance market, industry sources said on Monday.

A senior Japanese Finance Ministry official (MOF) said in Washington that Japan has already told the United States that it may delay Japanese insurance subsidiaries' entry into the so-called third-sector market until January 1.
Japan's life and non-life insurance companies can enter each others' business through subsidiaries from Tuesday under a Japanese law on the insurance market enacted in April.
Earlier this month, 11 Japanese non-life insurance companies and six life insurance firms set up subsidiaries to enter each other's business.
Previously, insurance companies could operate only in one business sector.
"We are very sorry that we cannot start selling certain policies of the so-called third sector insurance policies," said an official at a life insurance company.

Japan and the United States agreed in 1994 that the implementation of the new insurance business law will not lead to any radical change in the third-sector market, which covers such items as personal accident, sickness and nursing care -- the stronghold of foreign insurers.
However, Washington was unhappy with the proposed opening of this sector under the revised insurance law.

The Finance Ministry has warned the insurance industry that it would probably take steps to restrict the range of business in the third-sector insurance market, depending on the development in Japan-U.S. insurance trade talks.

However, Japan and the United States still remain far apart on solving the dispute, and an agreement may be unlikely ahead of elections both in the United States and Japan, the MOF official said in Washington.
The U.S. presidential election is scheduled for November 5, while elections for Japan's Lower House of parliament are to be held on October 20.

Meanwhile, the government is considering deregulatory measures for the country's non-life insurance sector, such as lifting a ban on mail-order sales of auto insurance policies, industry sources said.
The change would help foreign companies, who do not have a large network of agents to do business.
But the ministry did not include any steps in the package to deregulate the current system of setting premium rates for auto insurance, the industry sources said.
Japanese non-life insurance companies have expressed strong concern over any further liberalisation in the way premium rates are set for car insurance policies.
